newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian buyers accept Saudi A-180 naphtha term price.
newsitem.headline: Asian buyers accept Saudi A-180 naphtha term price.

text.p: Some Asian buyers have accepted Saudi Aramco's term price for A-180 paraffinic naphtha lifting July 1997-June 1998, traders said on Tuesday.
But other potential buyers might drop out or have volumes cut amid difficulties in accepting Aramco's price for full-range naphtha, they said.

"Most firms in the talks are likely to have accepted the $17 per tonne premium (over the Aramco formula) for A-180 ahead of May 21 validity date," a Japanese trader said on the tender which closed April 4.

Traders said two existing term holders have agreed to the A-180 premium, and two newcomers have agreed to take up a package of A-180 and full-range naphtha at $17.00 and $15.00 per tonne respectively.
Talks held in Singapore last week had reached a deadlock by Friday, with buyers willing to meet Aramco's record high $17 target offer for the A-180 ethylene-rich feedstock from Ras Tanura.
But they were not willing to agree to the $15-premium for the low-paraffinic full-range material from Jubail and Rabigh.
The term contract volumes are renewed yearly at the middle of the year with a price review held just before of the end of each year, traders said.

Aramco has pressed for higher prices on the back of Asia's growing demand for naphtha as a petrochemical feedstock. Under contracts currently running for the first half of 1997, A-180 naphtha is priced at a premium of $6.50 per tonne, while full-range is priced at $5.50 to $5.80.
In the current talks, traders said Aramco has requested buyers take a package of the two grades, but some buyers preferred lifting A-180 grade only.

"The $15.00 premium for Jubail (full-range) was accepted by some firms...mainly to secure the A-180.. and rejected by others," a trader said. "Aramco is believed to have cut the A-180 allocation substantially for those firms who didn't accept the $15.00 premium."

Another trader said some buyers could bow out of the deal as they were unwilling to accept the package of the two grades while others were still negotiating on the quantity of full-range naphtha they were willing to lift.
Traders expected around three million tonnes of A-180 to be allocated for the one-year period, while the amount of full-range naphtha could range between 1.2 million and three million tonnes.
"Everything will be clearer tomorrow," a trader said.
With contribution from Kiyoshi Tanaka in Tokyo.
